profile.summary: ProtBert is a protein language model with the BERT architecture, trained only on protein sequences with a masked language modelling objective: 15 per cent of the amino acids in a sequence are hidden and the model learns to put them back. It takes an uppercase amino-acid sequence, written with a space between residues, and returns either predictions for the masked positions or a vector per residue, 1024 numbers wide, that can be used as a feature for another model. The developers say it can be used for feature extraction or fine-tuned on a downstream task, and that fine-tuning was more accurate on some tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: ProtBert model, Model description, Intended uses & limitations, How to use; config.json

summary_quotes.text: Pretrained model on protein sequences using a masked language modeling (MLM) objective.
The masking follows the original Bert training with randomly masks 15% of the amino acids in the input.
This model is trained on uppercase amino acids: it only works with capital letter amino acids.

The model could be used for protein feature extraction or to be fine-tuned on downstream tasks.
We have noticed in some tasks you could gain more accuracy by fine-tuning the model rather than using it as a feature extractor.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The architecture is BERT, declared in the config as BertForMaskedLM with 30 hidden layers, a hidden size of 1024, 16 attention heads, an intermediate size of 4096 and a vocabulary of 30 tokens. Unlike the original BERT there is no next-sentence prediction, because each protein sequence is treated as a complete document. Masking follows the original recipe: 15 per cent of amino acids are chosen, 80 per cent of those are replaced by the mask token, 10 per cent by a different random amino acid and 10 per cent left as they are. Sequences are uppercased and split with single spaces, and the rare letters U, Z, O and B are mapped to X. Training ran on one TPU Pod V3-512 for 400,000 steps, 300,000 at sequence length 512 with batch size 15k and 100,000 at length 2048 with batch size 2.5k, with the Lamb optimiser at learning rate 0.002.

quotes.text: This means the Next sentence prediction is not used, as each sequence is treated as a complete document.

- 15% of the amino acids are masked.
- In 80% of the cases, the masked amino acids are replaced by `[MASK]`.
The protein sequences are uppercased and tokenized using a single space and a vocabulary size of 21. The rare amino acids "U,Z,O,B" were mapped to "X".

The model was trained on a single TPU Pod V3-512 for 400k steps in total.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two BERT checkpoints exist in the ProtTrans family and they differ in their training corpus: ProtBert, trained on UniRef100, and ProtBert-BFD, trained on BFD. The paper gives both the same 30-layer architecture; ProtBert was trained for 300k steps at length 512 and 100k at length 2048, ProtBert-BFD for 800k and then 200k steps at the same two lengths. A result should say which one, since the ProtTrans README reports different downstream numbers for them, for example 75 against 76 on CASP12 three-state secondary structure. Each is published both on the Hugging Face hub and on Zenodo, and neither is gated. The Hugging Face revisions read here are 7a894481acdc12202f0a415dd567f6cfdb698908 for ProtBert and 6c5c8a55a52ff08a664dfd584aa1773f125a0487 for ProtBert-BFD. The wider ProtTrans release also holds ProtT5, ProtAlbert, ProtXLNet and ProtElectra models, which are different architectures and not covered here.

sections.title: Licensing: code and weights differ
sections.body: The ProtTrans repository code is MIT. The pretrained models are not: the README states they are released under the Academic Free License v3.0. The Hugging Face repository for ProtBert declares no licence at all in its card metadata, so the README is the only statement of terms for the weights. Anyone redistributing or building a product on the weights should read the Academic Free License itself rather than assume the repository's MIT terms apply to them.

run_guide.summary: Load ProtBert from the Hugging Face hub and get a vector per residue for one sequence.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and the transformers library. The model card does not pin versions.
The weights download from the hub on first use; they are not gated.
No GPU requirement is stated in the sources read.
The weights are under the Academic Free License v3.0, not the repository's MIT licence.

steps.title: Install the libraries
steps.explanation: The ProtTrans README's installation section names transformers, torch and sentencepiece. sentencepiece is only needed for the T5 models but is listed with them.

quotes.text: For more details, please follow the instructions for [transformers installations](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/installation).

steps.title: Get features for one sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import BertModel, BertTokenizer
import re
tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_bert", do_lower_case=False )
model = BertModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_bert")
sequence_Example = "A E T C Z A O"
sequence_Example = re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence_Example)
encoded_input = tokenizer(sequence_Example, return_tensors='pt')
output = model(**encoded_input)
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's own feature extraction example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the tokenizer and weights, rewrites the rare residues, tokenises the spaced sequence and runs one forward pass.

steps.title: Or predict a masked residue
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import BertForMaskedLM, BertTokenizer, pipeline
tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_bert", do_lower_case=False )
model = BertForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_bert")
unmasker = pipeline('fill-mask', model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer)
print(unmasker('D L I P T S S K L V V [MASK] D T S L Q V K K A F F A L V T'))
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's fill-mask example, wrapped in a shell heredoc, with a print added so the result is shown. The card's own output lists L, S, V, K and I as the top five candidates with their scores.
